title: Matthew 17:1–8
context: Six days after Peter’s confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured; Moses and Elijah appear; the Father’s voice from the bright cloud commands them to listen to the beloved Son. The disciples fall in fear; Jesus touches them, and they see Jesus only.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on revelation, the beloved Son, and listening to Christ, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: I ascribe to grace the commencement, the continuance and the consummation of all good… according to the scriptures, many persons resist the Holy Spirit and reject the grace that is offered.
Hear ye him—As if he had said, Hear not Moses, or Elijah: they were only servants; hear Him, who is my beloved Son.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 17:5)

reformed.quote: Listen to him. These words are very emphatic; for they mean that… we must listen to him alone… The Father commands us to listen to him alone.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 17:5)

reformed.quote: Why is he called God’s only begotten Son, when we also are children of God? Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God. We, however, are children of God by adoption, through grace, for Christ’s sake.

verses.text: After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves.
verses.arminianNotes:
After the hard word of the cross (16:21–28), Jesus grants a selected three a mountain vision. Grace often prepares faith with both warning and wonder.

God sincerely strengthens disciples for the road ahead. The invitation upward is gift; they must still climb in obedient trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Timing (“after six days”) ties glory to the passion path already announced. Christ chooses witnesses according to His purpose.

Revelation is scheduled by the Lord, not seized by the crowd. What they will see is preparation for Gethsemane and the cross.

verses.text: He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.
verses.arminianNotes:
The veiled glory of the Son briefly shines. Disciples glimpse who has been walking with them in ordinary flesh.

Arminian readers rejoice that God makes Christ known so that faith may rest on a Person. The light is given to be received, not earned by spiritual achievement.
verses.reformedNotes:
Metamorphosis before them: the Son’s majesty breaks through. This is not borrowed radiance but His own.

The same Lord who will suffer is already glorious. Faith is steadied by God’s disclosure of who Jesus truly is.

verses.text: Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Law and Prophets stand with Jesus—not as rivals, but as witnesses. The conversation centers on Jesus.

All prior revelation leads to Christ and still calls for a living response. Scripture’s storyline presses hearers toward the Son.
verses.reformedNotes:
Moses and Elijah appear as servants flanking the Master. Redemptive history converges on this mountain.

The covenant Word finds its goal in Christ. God Himself arranges the scene so that Jesus is not one prophet among equals.

verses.text: Peter answered and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Peter’s zeal is sincere and confused. Equal tents would flatten the hierarchy the Father is about to declare.

Warm religious impulse still needs correcting by grace. Loving Jesus does not exempt us from learning His unique place.
verses.reformedNotes:
“If you want, let’s” sounds humble, yet the plan levels Christ with Moses and Elijah. Affection can still mis-order glory.

Even favored disciples need the Father’s voice to reorder their theology. Christ will not share equal booths with the servants.

verses.text: While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Father interrupts Peter’s building plan. Identity (“beloved Son”) and command (“listen to him”) are the heart of the vision.

Arminian interpreters hear an earnest summons to all: grace reveals the Son and enables obedience; hearers remain responsible to listen rather than silence Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Shekinah cloud and heavenly voice seal Jesus’ identity. Pleasure and belovedness echo the baptism; the added “listen” crowns the revelation.

Saving knowledge of the Son is the Father’s gift and charge. The church lives under this royal command.
verses.keyContrast: Both receive the Father’s word as decisive. Arminians typically emphasize grace that enables an obedient hearing of the Son; Reformed readers stress the Father’s effectual revelation that secures true listening in His people.

verses.text: When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid.
verses.arminianNotes:
Holy fear is the right first response to the Father’s voice. Proximity to glory undoes casual religion.

Conviction and awe prepare the heart for the comfort Jesus will give. Grace both humbles and restores.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hearing produces prostration. Sinners cannot stand unshaken before unveiled majesty.

True revelation includes holy dread. God is not managed; disciples are undone before they are lifted.

verses.text: Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The same Jesus who shines in glory comes near with a human touch. Comfort follows command.

The Son who must be heard is also the Savior who raises the fearful. Grace invites rising trust, not paralysis.
verses.reformedNotes:
Incarnate kindness meets holy terror. Touch and word together restore the witnesses.

The Mediator stands between glory and frailty. He who is the beloved Son also shepherds trembling disciples.

verses.text: Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses and Elijah vanish; the vision ends with Jesus alone. The point was never equal tents but exclusive attention to the Son.

Christian life keeps lifting the eyes to Christ. Grace continually recenters faith on Him alone for salvation and obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Jesus alone” is the theological summary of the mountain. Servants withdraw; the Son remains.

All lesser lights yield to Christ. The church’s hope, hearing, and holiness are fixed on Him alone.
